frictionVectors.title: European Gas Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and uses pipeline and LNG exports to preserve leverage with Europe. European diversification efforts and price volatility constrain that influence.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: External Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Angola remains heavily dependent on foreign operators, oil revenues, and external finance despite efforts to strengthen national participation and diversify production.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting US, European, Chinese, and Gulf interest because of its access to Congolese and Zambian copper-cobalt. Infrastructure financing could expand Angola's leverage but also deepen dependency on competing external blocs.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou-Niamey Trade Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain strained over border and transit restrictions, reducing the regional value of Benin's port infrastructure and disrupting trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Insurgency Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity from the Sahel threatens northern transport routes and raises the cost of protecting energy, mining, and agricultural infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position with De Beers, but diamond-market weakness and reliance on external marketing networks still limit full sovereign control over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: New-Mineral Investment Terms
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and rare-earth projects creates diversification opportunities while testing Botswana's ability to secure local processing and durable fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Sovereignty Push
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state control and local processing of gold, but weak oversight, informal mining, and insecurity make revenue capture difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Growing reliance on Russian-linked security assistance reduces Western influence but introduces new dependency risks and uncertainty around access to strategic mining assets.

highlights: Mining ambitions meet weak state capacity
Rwanda ties remain a sovereignty pressure point

frictionVectors.title: Cross-border security tensions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over alleged support to armed groups in eastern DRC and contested border-security narratives. The dispute limits regional trade and complicates Burundi's independent security posture.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel, rare-earth, and other mineral projects, but financing, processing capacity, and foreign technical dependence constrain value capture.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, airports, digital networks, and renewable-energy projects rely heavily on foreign capital and development partners. This expands connectivity while limiting purely national control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic security competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's location attracts cooperation from European, North American, and regional actors on maritime surveillance and transshipment control. The government must balance security partnerships without becoming a proxy platform.

highlights: Ports and pipelines anchor external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Strategic transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Kribi and Douala port systems, oil infrastructure, and major road corridors remain central to foreign commercial influence. Financing and operating arrangements can reduce domestic bargaining power despite state ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside insurgent threats in the Far North, disrupts local economies and weakens state oversight of land, timber, and border trade. External security partnerships provide support but also reinforce dependence.

highlights: Russian security partnership reshapes state authority

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked operators and armed networks compete for control of mining zones, while weak regulation limits public revenue and local benefits. The government faces persistent pressure to trade concessions for security or political support.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain important to regime protection and military operations, creating leverage over strategic decisions and resource access. This relationship narrows Bangui's room to diversify external partnerships.

highlights: Oil finances a tightly managed transition

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenue remains central to state finances, while foreign operators, export infrastructure, and opaque fiscal arrangements constrain domestic control. Volatility and production disputes expose the government to external bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government continues to rely on external military and diplomatic backing while managing insurgency and political opposition. The conflict in neighboring Sudan adds refugee, arms-trafficking, and cross-border militia pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and Maritime Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: France's control of Mayotte continues to limit Comoros' practical sovereignty claims and complicate maritime resource management, migration policy, and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country remains reliant on externally financed port, energy, and telecommunications projects, leaving limited domestic leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Mining and Armed Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to weaken state control over mineral-producing areas and enables illicit cross-border extraction involving armed groups and regional networks.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and regional actors are competing for access to cobalt, copper, and other critical minerals, while Kinshasa seeks better terms and greater domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export earnings remain heavily exposed to offshore oil production, foreign operators, and commodity-price volatility, limiting policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese participation in roads, ports, and extractive projects provides essential capital but can constrain transparency and increase dependence on external contractors and creditors.

highlights: Abidjan is becoming a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire retains limited control over pricing, processing, and global standards in the cocoa chain, despite efforts to expand domestic transformation and producer revenues.

frictionVectors.title: External Energy and Port Capital
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment remains important to offshore gas, power, and port expansion, creating manageable but persistent concerns over concession terms and strategic dependence.

highlights: Foreign bases underpin the economic model
Ethiopian trade dependence raises leverage risks

frictionVectors.title: Port and Military Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's strategic ports and military facilities are dominated by long-term foreign leases and operating agreements, generating revenue while constraining sovereign control over critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Ethiopian Corridor Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Ethiopian transit demand makes Djibouti vulnerable to shifts in Ethiopia's port strategy, regional instability, and competition from alternative Red Sea and Gulf corridors.

highlights: Suez and gas remain strategic bargaining chips

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions, Gulf investment and major asset sales are expanding foreign influence over strategic sectors. Debt servicing and currency pressure constrain Cairo's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and canal security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict around the Red Sea and Gaza threatens Suez Canal revenues and forces Egypt to balance maritime security with regional diplomacy.

highlights: Gas monetization seeks a second wind

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil output and volatile prices leave the state reliant on foreign operators, LNG infrastructure and external technical capital. Resource control remains centralized but economically vulnerable.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime boundary competition
frictionVectors.details: Overlapping Gulf of Guinea interests and offshore development create recurring legal and diplomatic friction with neighboring states, particularly around hydrocarbons and fisheries.

highlights: Mining remains the main external gateway
Red Sea leverage exceeds economic weight

frictionVectors.title: Mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper and zinc projects provide essential foreign exchange but expose Eritrea to concentrated foreign investment and opaque revenue-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Regional competition involving Ethiopia, Gulf actors and maritime powers increases pressure on Eritrean ports and sovereignty. Asmara seeks leverage while resisting durable external alignment.

highlights: South African systems underpin the economy
Sugar and manufacturing retain local leverage

frictionVectors.title: South African dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, energy, transport and monetary links with South Africa provide stability but sharply limit Eswatini's strategic autonomy and expose it to regional economic shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Road, power and industrial projects depend on external lenders and regional supply chains. Financing needs can reinforce political and commercial influence from neighboring states and foreign partners.

highlights: Debt and conflict narrow strategic room

frictionVectors.title: Nile negotiations
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam enhances control over domestic power and water infrastructure, but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, currency reform and dependence on external financing give international creditors and partners greater leverage over infrastructure and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: French and Chinese competition
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is seeking more local value addition and diversified partnerships in oil, manganese, and infrastructure, while established French interests and expanding Chinese financing remain influential.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors linking mines to Owendo and other ports remain strategically important, leaving Gabon exposed to external contractors, financing conditions, and logistical bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and trade exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia remains economically and geographically dependent on Senegal, particularly for transit, energy, and security cooperation, limiting policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign-linked fleets continues to create sovereignty and food-security concerns, while weak monitoring capacity constrains enforcement in Gambian waters.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey undermines water security, agricultural land, and state authority, while political pressure complicates enforcement against domestic and foreign-linked operators.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms constrain fiscal room, even as Accra seeks stronger terms for gold, bauxite, and emerging lithium partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: The railway, port, and mining corridor is increasing Guinea's export potential but also deepening dependence on large Chinese- and multinational-led consortia.

frictionVectors.title: Political transition uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military authorities retain tight control over political space and mining negotiations, creating uncertainty over contracts, local participation, and long-term sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cashew trade
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on raw cashew exports leaves producers vulnerable to foreign buyers, price shocks, and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Narco-trafficking and port weakness
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement sustain the country's exposure to transnational trafficking networks, undermining sovereign control over ports and coastal waters.

highlights: Geothermal expansion strengthens domestic energy resilience
Debt and port politics constrain strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Sovereign Debt and External Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations and reliance on IMF-supported financing narrow Nairobi's policy space. Chinese lending exposure and Western financial conditions remain central to infrastructure and budget decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Lamu corridor remain contested strategic assets, with Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests competing for influence over logistics, energy, and regional trade routes.

highlights: Water exports remain the kingdom's core strategic asset
Economic dependence on South Africa persists

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water revenues and major dam infrastructure are tightly linked to South African demand and financing. Delays, cost overruns, and disputes over royalties expose the kingdom to asymmetric bargaining pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Customs and Labor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on South African markets, remittances, and regional customs arrangements limits independent economic policymaking. Textile-sector access and labor mobility remain vulnerable to external regulatory shifts.

highlights: Mining investment is reviving export capacity
Concession politics test control over national assets

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Port Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining and logistics operators retain substantial influence over iron ore production, rail links, and port access. The government is seeking greater fiscal returns and local value addition without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Road, energy, and port development remains dependent on external donors, lenders, and concessionaires. This creates leverage for foreign partners over project sequencing and long-term resource access.

highlights: Oil remains divided among rival political centers
Foreign military and energy actors shape national leverage

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival authorities and armed networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and revenue distribution. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and political bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Footprints
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked networks, and other external actors retain influence through security partnerships, bases, and energy interests. Their presence limits unified Libyan control over strategic infrastructure and borders.

highlights: Critical minerals attract escalating foreign competition
Weak state capacity limits domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms dominate major nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and gemstone projects, giving external investors substantial influence over production and export terms. Fiscal gains remain constrained by infrastructure, governance, and bargaining weaknesses.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and Energy Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign capital for ports, roads, and power infrastructure increases exposure to investor conditions and project delays. Unreliable domestic energy supply also weakens local processing and sovereignty over mineral value chains.

highlights: Energy and fertilizer dependence remain binding

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of emerging mining projects
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in rare earths, graphite and uranium, but limited domestic capital and regulatory capacity leave the state vulnerable to unfavorable ownership and offtake terms.

frictionVectors.title: Power and fuel import exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and dependence on imported fuel constrain industrial sovereignty, while external lenders and donors retain significant influence over infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Resource nationalism strengthens under military rule
Gold sector faces widening geopolitical competition

frictionVectors.title: Junta pressure on foreign mining operators
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is demanding greater state participation and revenue from gold projects, increasing tensions with international operators and raising legal and operational uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support expands Moscow's influence over strategic decision-making while Western sanctions, diplomatic isolation and insecurity restrict alternative partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance of extractive infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas and iron-ore sectors are generating new state revenue, but major foreign operators and export infrastructure still control much of the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Atlantic security pressures
frictionVectors.details: Mauritania's relative stability is valuable to external partners, yet instability in neighboring Mali and competition around Atlantic logistics create persistent sovereignty and border-management risks.

highlights: Indian Ocean positioning raises external competition

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty and basing uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved transition over sovereignty and security arrangements in the Chagos Archipelago keeps Mauritius exposed to British and broader Western strategic interests in the Indian Ocean.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in food and energy
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control, but its import dependence for fuel, food and maritime logistics limits resilience during global supply disruptions.

highlights: Phosphate and green-industry strategy expands leverage
Atlantic and Mediterranean corridors deepen influence

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries and infrastructure development to consolidate control over Western Sahara, while recognition disputes continue to generate diplomatic and legal friction.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf and Chinese investment accelerates ports, renewables and manufacturing, but creates exposure to external financing priorities and competing geopolitical alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Development
frictionVectors.details: Major gas projects remain dependent on international operators, lenders, and security guarantees, limiting Mozambique's near-term bargaining power and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and Coastal Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence in Cabo Delgado continues to threaten LNG facilities, transport corridors, and local legitimacy despite regional and international security support.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Prospects
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate offshore oil exploration and emerging green-hydrogen projects, creating opportunities for revenue but also risks of weak local participation and fiscal leakage.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Power Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Limited water, electricity, and port capacity could constrain industrial ambitions and increase reliance on foreign capital and regional supply networks.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Oil Contract Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater control over uranium, oil, and mining terms while confronting the commercial and diplomatic costs of strained relations with Western operators.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from Western military support toward Russian and regional partnerships may preserve regime security but risks worsening insurgency, border instability, and infrastructure vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is improving regulatory control and attracting investment, but offshore production, LNG, financing, and technology remain heavily dependent on multinational firms.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Grid Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, sabotage, insecurity, and unreliable electricity infrastructure continue to erode public revenue and limit sovereign control over strategic energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Linked Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo generate persistent scrutiny over supply-chain transparency and sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Investment Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Ambitious infrastructure and technology programs remain supported by foreign aid, concessional finance, and external investors, giving partners influence over national development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Joint exploration with Nigeria has produced expectations but no commercially proven production, leaving São Tomé dependent on aid, tourism, and licensing revenues. Weak institutional capacity increases the risk of unfavorable future contracts.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and multilateral lenders remain important to infrastructure and budget support. This expands policy options but limits fiscal autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New oil and LNG revenues could strengthen state capacity, but contract reviews and local-content demands risk disputes with international operators and investors. Revenue transparency will determine whether production improves sovereignty or deepens elite capture.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing access and coastal security
frictionVectors.details: Industrial foreign fleets and persistent illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing pressure coastal livelihoods. Dakar is also balancing European maritime cooperation with demands for greater national control of fisheries.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles has improved fiscal management, but tourism dependence and external borrowing constrain sovereign room for maneuver. Infrastructure and finance links with India, China, and Gulf partners require careful balancing.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime resource enforcement
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago has strong incentives to protect fisheries, seabed resources, and its blue-economy brand, yet its vast maritime zone is difficult to police. Reliance on foreign naval and technical support creates a modest sovereignty vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concession risk
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects provide exports and jobs but can leave the state exposed to volatile prices, tax disputes, and environmental costs. Contract enforcement and local value addition remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of logistics
frictionVectors.details: Mining depends on externally financed ports, roads, power, and shipping arrangements, giving foreign firms leverage over national infrastructure. Freetown is seeking investment while trying to prevent strategic assets from becoming enclave corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Port diplomacy and federal tensions
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, and other external partners compete for access, security ties, and port influence along Somalia’s coast. Agreements involving federal member states can deepen internal disputes over who controls maritime assets and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-resources dependence
frictionVectors.details: Counterterrorism support and maritime protection remain heavily dependent on foreign forces, contractors, and donors. This limits autonomous control even as Somalia pursues offshore hydrocarbons and stronger management of fisheries.

highlights: Power and rail bottlenecks constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: MINING CAPITAL AND BENEFICIATION
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater local processing of platinum, manganese and other strategic minerals, while foreign investors and mining firms resist higher regulatory and ownership burdens.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS AND GRID FRAGILITY
frictionVectors.details: Electricity constraints and deteriorating rail and port networks weaken sovereign control over mineral exports and increase reliance on private operators and external capital.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the state’s lifeline
Export infrastructure is hostage to regional instability

frictionVectors.title: OIL TRANSIT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on pipelines and export facilities crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production and public finances vulnerable to external disruption and Sudanese bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE REVENUE OPACITY
frictionVectors.details: Limited institutional capacity, elite competition and opaque oil arrangements reduce national control over petroleum revenues and create openings for foreign intermediaries.

highlights: War fragments control of extractive assets
Gold remains central to wartime financing

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND EXTERNAL WAR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and associated commercial networks seek control of gold production and export channels, while foreign patrons deepen the conflict economy.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Damage and insecurity around transport corridors, Port Sudan and oil infrastructure threaten export sovereignty and leave the country dependent on external security and logistics support.

highlights: LNG and corridor projects reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG CONTRACTING AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pursuing major offshore gas development while negotiating terms that preserve state participation, domestic value capture and regulatory control against powerful international investors.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND EXPORT CORRIDORS
frictionVectors.details: New rail, port and mineral projects bring financing and market access but also raise concerns over concession terms, local processing and dependence on foreign operators.

highlights: Lomé strengthens its regional logistics role

frictionVectors.title: PORT-DEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major national asset and regional transshipment hub, but its expansion depends on foreign capital, concession expertise and exposure to shifting maritime trade patterns.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA SECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Togo relies on regional and international maritime-security cooperation to protect shipping and port revenues, limiting fully independent control of its coastal infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic sovereignty concerns are heightened by opaque implementation and conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons and reliance on cross-border electricity and gas arrangements. Fiscal stress limits the state's ability to accelerate renewable-energy sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline strengthens export infrastructure but remains constrained by environmental criticism, investor caution, and Western pressure. China and other non-Western partners are increasingly important to project execution.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects rely heavily on external lenders and contractors, narrowing fiscal room and bargaining autonomy. Kampala is diversifying partners while retaining strong dependence on Chinese capital and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership and value capture
frictionVectors.details: Rising copper demand gives Lusaka greater negotiating power, but foreign-owned mines, tax disputes, and limited domestic processing constrain sovereign value capture. Competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors is intensifying.

frictionVectors.title: External creditors and infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has stabilized Zambia's position but leaves policy space conditioned by creditors and international financial institutions. Transport and power bottlenecks continue to expose the copper sector to external infrastructure dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is seeking greater domestic processing and tighter control over lithium, platinum, and gold, but lacks sufficient capital, technology, and reliable power. Chinese firms remain central to investment and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, currency, and payment constraints
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, monetary instability, and restricted access to conventional finance raise transaction costs and weaken the state's bargaining position. Resource revenues remain vulnerable to opaque structures and external intermediaries.
